Nothing territorial is recorded 287-303: 'From 291 to 306, a series of civil wars known as the War of the Eight Princes were fought' without a frontier change. The independence of Cheng-Han and Han-Zhao is dated to 304 on the page ('In 304, the Cheng-Han and Han-Zhao declared their independence from Jin'), two years before Cliopatria's 306 shape, so this shape holds 287-303 and western-jin_304 carries 304-305. From 289 the Murong of the Liao are Jin vassals ('he submitted as a Jin vassal in 289', Murong Hui page; ledger): the 488 Liaoning cells of this shape are overlaid by that tint.

correction.text: Cliopatria's Western Jin shape of 306, held from 304

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 304-305: 'In 304, Li Xiong ousted Luo Shang from Chengdu, where he declared himself the King of Chengdu' and Liu Yuan 'proclaimed himself the King of Han' in 304 (Han-Zhao page), so the Sichuan Basin and the Fen valley leave the Jin two years before Cliopatria's 306 shape. Luo Shang's Jin forces still held part of Yi until his death in 310, which the contest events 301-310 record.

2,950,022 km2 (13,228 cells) for 306-307: the Western Regions go to Cliopatria's Protectorate row (2,407 cells; this dossier keeps them as a vassal tint to about 328), Yi to Cheng Han (1,850), the Fen valley to Former Zhao (1,328). 'Liu Yuan ... in 308, he elevated himself to Emperor of Han'; 'Li Xiong elevated himself to Emperor of Cheng in 306'. The shape stands; the cells in Han-Zhao's hands are larger than the page supports before 308 (Lishi in 304, Pingyang in 308).

The Shaanxi cells lie east of Chang'an, which the Jin kept until 316.

2,707,182 km2 (12,034 cells) for 313-323: Lelang goes to Goguryeo ('In 313, the territory of Lelang was annexed by Goguryeo under King Micheon'; Daifang in 314 on 'a single line'). The shape holds the Western Jin to the fall of Chang'an in 316; it cannot be the Eastern Jin of 317-323, whose court sat 'south of the Huai River' (Jin infobox) and is replaced from 317 by western-jin_317. Gansu (1,052 cells) is Zhang Gui's Liang Province, a Jin province until his death in 314.

correction.text: Cliopatria's Western Jin shape of 337, the Eastern Jin south of the Huai, held from 317

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 317-336: the Eastern Jin. The Jin page's infobox: 'Eastern Jin begins; evacuation south of the Huai River: 317'; of Sima Rui, 'He reestablished the Jin government at Jiankang'; the court was 'content with maintaining a border along or above the Huai river in the north' (Sixteen Kingdoms page). The shape is Cliopatria's 337 shape (1,888,346 km2, 7,930 cells: Hunan, Hubei, Jiangxi, Guangdong, Guangxi, Guizhou, Anhui south of the Huai, Fujian, Zhejiang), drawn from 317 at confidence 2: the pages do not date when Hebei, Shandong, Henan and the Huai country left (the Sixteen Kingdoms page has Shi Le found the Later Zhao 'In 319' and destroy the Han-Zhao 'in 329, placing most of northern China under his control'). Gansu and Liaoning are drawn as vassal tints: Zhang Gui's heirs, who 'nominally retained their status as Jin officials' (Former Liang page), until 323; the Murong, who 'professed their allegiance to the Eastern Jin', until 352, when 'Murong Jun thereupon broke away from the Eastern Jin' (Sixteen Kingdoms page).

correction.text: not used as drawn; the Eastern Jin of 324-336 is the 337 shape, western-jin_317

keyframe_review.note: 2,401,498 km2 (10,729 cells) for 324-336: the 313 shape without Gansu, which Cliopatria's Former Liang takes in 324 (1,304 cells). It still holds Hebei, Shandong, Liaoning and the Henan and Huai country (2,799 cells) until 337, but Later Zhao 'destroyed the Han-Zhao in 329, placing most of northern China under his control' and the Murong of the Liao were Jin's vassals; the Eastern Jin of 317-336 is western-jin_317.

1,888,346 km2 (7,930 cells) for 337-346: Cliopatria hands Hebei, Shandong, Liaoning and the Huai country (2,726 cells) to other states in 337, but most of that ground is the Later Zhao's, not the Former Yan's: Shi Le 'destroyed the Han-Zhao in 329, placing most of northern China under his control', and the Former Yan beat Ran Min, who had replaced the Later Zhao, only in 352 ('In 352, his brother, Murong Ke defeated and captured Ran Min at the Battle of Liantai'). Liaoning is the Murong's: 'In 337, while still claiming to be a vassal of Jin, their chieftain, Murong Huang took the title of Prince' (Sixteen Kingdoms page); the Murong stay Jin vassals on this dossier's ledger to 352. The Jin infobox gives 2.8 M km2 for 347 (the Eastern Jin's peak); this shape is 0.67 of it, the 347 shape 0.84.

2,339,997 km2 (9,784 cells) for 347-370: Sichuan returns from Cheng Han ('in 347, he reached Chengdu and forced Li Shi to surrender, ending the Cheng-Han dynasty'); 2.34 M km2 against the Jin infobox's 2.8 M km2 for 347: ratio 0.84. Huan Wen's expeditions (354 against Former Qin, 356 Luoyang, 369 Fangtou) left no permanent change; Luoyang is held 356-364 in western-jin_356.

ledger.note: 352: Murong Jun breaks away. 'In 352, his brother, Murong Ke defeated and captured Ran Min at the Battle of Liantai.' 'Murong Jun thereupon broke away from the Eastern Jin and proclaimed himself as emperor.' Murong Huang had taken the title of Prince in 337 'while still claiming to be a vassal of Jin' and founded the Former Yan (337-370), so the tint runs to 352 (it ended in 337 before).

region.text: Guanzhong: the Wei valley round Chang'an

ledger.note: 354: Huan Wen's northern expedition. 'Huan launched a major attack against one of Later Zhao's successor states, Former Qin, in 354'; his army reached the vicinity of Chang'an and withdrew for lack of food.

region.text: Guanzhong: the Wei valley round Chang'an

ledger.note: 354: the army withdraws from Guanzhong for lack of food.

region.text: Luoyang and the Henan plain round it

ledger.note: 356: Huan Wen retakes Luoyang. 'Huan advanced his troops to Luoyang and faced Yao in battle. He defeated Yao Xiang and secured the Luoyang region for Jin.' The sentence carries no year; the paragraph is fixed by 'In 356, Huan submitted a petition requesting that the capital be moved back'.

region.text: Luoyang and the Henan plain round it

ledger.note: 365: Luoyang falls to Murong Ke. 'In 365, Murong Ke attacked Luoyang ... Soon, Luoyang fell.'

region.text: Fangtou on the Yellow River

ledger.note: 369: Huan Wen's expedition against Former Yan. 'In 369, he launched the campaign'; he stopped at Fangtou and suffered 'his greatest defeat' in the trap of Murong Chui and Murong De.

region.text: Fangtou on the Yellow River

ledger.note: 369: the defeat at Fangtou ends the campaign without a change of frontier.

region.text: Sichuan and Chongqing, Liang and Yi provinces

ledger.note: 373: Former Qin takes Sichuan. 'In 373 seized modern Sichuan and Chongqing from Jin.'

region.text: Xiangyang, gateway to the Middle Yangtze

ledger.note: 379: Xiangyang falls. 'In 379, the strategically important city of Xiangyang, gateway to the Middle Yangtze, fell to Qin.'

region.text: the lands south of the Yellow River and Sichuan recovered after the Fei River

ledger.note: 383: the Jin recovers its losses. 'Early on, the Jin lost Sichuan in 373 and then the major city of Xiangyang in 379 ... were able to recover them and push the Former Qin back all the way to the Yellow River' (Sixteen Kingdoms); 'Jin recaptures territories south of the Yellow River' (Fei River infobox). The year is the battle's; the recovery took the following months.

region.text: the Fei River and Shouyang on the Huai

ledger.note: 383: the Fei River. The battle 'took place in the autumn of 383 AD'; 'In November 383, the Former Qin troops set up camp west of the' river; infobox 30 November 383. Shouyang had fallen in October.

region.text: the Fei River and Shouyang on the Huai

ledger.note: 383: 'Decisive Jin victory' at the Fei River; the Former Qin 'fell into a massive civil war'.

region.text: Hebei and Henan cells that Cliopatria draws as Jin for 390-393

ledger.note: 390: Cliopatria's shape adds 276 cells of Hebei and Henan from the Former Qin; the Fei River page is silent on it, and so is the Later Yan page, which puts the Zhai Wei, a Dingling state, 'at Huatai (滑台, in modern Anyang, Henan) in 388' until Chui 'destroyed Zhai Wei' in 392: these cells may have been the Zhai Wei's, not the Jin's.

region.text: Hebei and Henan cells that Cliopatria draws as Jin for 390-393

ledger.note: 394: those cells go to Later Yan, which 'extinguished the Zhai Wei in 392 and conquered the Western Yan in 394' (Sixteen Kingdoms page) and had by 394 'recover[ed] most of their old territory in Liaoning, Hebei, Shaanxi, Shandong and Henan' (Later Yan page); the Jin's loss is Cliopatria's, not a page's.

region.text: Shandong, which Later Yan generals capture from the Eastern Jin after 394

ledger.note: 394: Shandong goes to Later Yan. 'Then, he sent his generals to capture Shandong from the Eastern Jin dynasty, bringing the state to its peak' (Later Yan page); the sentence follows 'In 394 ... Chui began a campaign to conquer Western Yan' and has no year of its own, so 394 is the page's sequence (confidence 2). Cliopatria draws Shandong as the Later Yan's from 387; the Jin keeps it to 393 here (western-jin_387 and _390).
403: Huan Xuan usurps the throne. 'In winter 403, Huan Xuan forced Emperor An of Jin to yield the throne to him, establishing the new state of Chu.'
404: Liu Yu overthrows Huan Xuan and restores the Jin ('after leading a rebellion in 404 to overthrow Huan Xuan').

region.text: Yi Province: Sichuan and Chongqing

ledger.note: 405: Qiao Zong's Western Shu secedes. 'In spring 405, Mao Qu's soldiers, unhappy that Mao sent them on long-distance campaigns' rebelled, 'defeated and killed Mao and captured Chengdu', and 'Qiao Zong established his independent Western Shu state there' (Emperor Wu of Liu Song page). The Western Shu page: 'Qiao Zong assumed the title Prince of Chengdu, and set his capital at Chengdu, the capital of Yi Province'; the Jin page: 'Western Shu became an independent kingdom under Qiao Zong'. Yi Province as Sichuan and Chongqing is my reading.

region.text: Shandong, the Southern Yan's

ledger.note: 409: Liu Yu marches on the Southern Yan. 'In 409-410, he led Jin forces to defeat and destroy the Southern Yan, thus recapturing the Shandong.'

region.text: Shandong, the Southern Yan's ground

ledger.note: 410: Shandong returns. 'In spring 410, Liu Yu captured Guanggu, ending Southern Yan.'

region.text: Shandong, the Southern Yan's

ledger.note: 410: Southern Yan ends.

region.text: Yi Province: Sichuan and Chongqing

ledger.note: Late 412: Liu Yu sends Zhu Lingshi against the Western Shu. 'Meanwhile, in late 412, Liu Yu commissioned the general Zhu Lingshi to attack Qiao Zong's Western Shu.' The page gives the commission, not the first battle; the earlier attack under Liu Jingxuan (407, stalled in 408) took no ground and is the war's start, not a contest.

region.text: Yi Province: Sichuan and Chongqing

ledger.note: 413: Western Shu is taken back. Zhu Lingshi's forces took Chengdu, 'capturing Chengdu in 413 and annexing Western Shu back into Jin' (Emperor Wu of Liu Song page); the Western Shu page has Qiao Zong abandon Chengdu and flee, and gives no month. Mirror of the 405 loss; western-jin_405 to _412 leave the land out of the shape.

region.text: Yi Province: Sichuan and Chongqing

ledger.note: 413: Chengdu falls and Western Shu ends, 'capturing Chengdu in 413 and annexing Western Shu back into Jin'.

Guanzhong: the Wei valley round Chang'an

region.text: Luoyang and Guanzhong, Later Qin's

ledger.note: 416: Liu Yu's northern expedition. 'In winter 416, the important city Luoyang fell to Liu Yu's general Tan Daoji'; the Sixteen Kingdoms page: he 'invaded Henan and captured Luoyang before turning towards the Guanzhong and seizing Chang'an'.

region.text: Luoyang, Guanzhong and the Henan and Wei valleys taken from Later Qin

ledger.note: 417: Chang'an falls. 'Wang Zhen'e's fleet then arrived and defeated Later Qin's final resistance, entering Chang'an' (spring 417; the page gives no month).

union.text: Luoyang and the Henan plain round it
Guanzhong: the Wei valley round Chang'an

region.text: Luoyang and Guanzhong, Later Qin's

ledger.note: 417: Later Qin ends.

region.text: Guanzhong: the Wei valley round Chang'an

ledger.note: 418: Xia strikes at Chang'an. Liu Yizhen's forces 'were crushed by Xia at Qingni'. The page gives no year; the Sixteen Kingdoms page has Helian Bobo seizing Guanzhong 'as Liu Yu returned to the south in 418'.

region.text: Guanzhong: the Wei valley round Chang'an

ledger.note: 418: Xia takes Guanzhong. 'Helian Bobo took the opportunity to seize the Guanzhong region as Liu Yu returned to the south in 418'; 'the Chang'an region became Xia possession, although Jin retained the Luoyang region' (Liu Yu page).

region.text: Guanzhong: the Wei valley round Chang'an

ledger.note: 418: Liu Yu abandons his plans against Xia; the frontier stays.

minus.text: Guanzhong: the Wei valley round Chang'an

region.text: the Eastern Jin's last land, without Guanzhong

ledger.note: 420: Liu Yu ends the Jin. 'In 420, he forced Emperor Gong of Jin to yield the throne to him, thus ending the Eastern Jin dynasty'; Liu Yu crowned himself on the dingmao day of the sixth month, 10 July 420 (Julian), and took the throne three days later, founding the Liu Song.

wars.outcome: 'A series of civil wars' that 'weakened it considerably'; no frontier changed, but Cheng-Han and Han-Zhao rose in 304.

Hanzhong

wars.outcome: Li Te's rebellion from 301, Li Xiong king of Chengdu in 304 and emperor in 306, Luo Shang dead in 310, Hanzhong ceded in 314.

Luoyang and the Henan plain round it

wars.name: Linyi (Lâm Ấp) attacks on Jin Jiaozhou

zones.text: Rinan north of Huế to the Hoành Sơn range

wars.outcome: 'In 347, king Fan Wen (范文) attacked Jin-controlled Jiaozhou with 40–50,000 troops'; in 399 Bhadravarman 'tried to seize the coast of Jiaozhou and Rinan'; in 413 he 'attacked Jiao again, but was defeated, captured and beheaded by the Governor of Jiaozhou, Du Xuedu'. The page records no change of frontier, so no loss is entered here against champa's 347 gain of northern Rinan (confidence 1 there).
wars.note: The Lâm Ấp page also has 'Lâm Ấp itself resorted from 323 to seaborne raids on northern ports in Jiaozhou'. Cliopatria's Jin shapes keep Quảng Bình (26 of 28 cells) to 417.

zones.text: Guanzhong: the Wei valley round Chang'an
Luoyang and the Henan plain round it
Fangtou

wars.name: Sun En's rebellion

zones.text: Kuaiji (modern Shaoxing), which Sun En captured
Panyu (modern Guangzhou), which Lu Xun captured in 404

wars.outcome: Sun En 'captured Kuaiji' and fled to Zhoushan Island; Liu Yu beat him at Haiyan in winter 401 and he died in battle in 401 (Emperor Wu page) or 'April or May 402' (Sun En page). Lu Xun succeeded him, attacked Dongyang in 403, 'in 404 marched south and captured Panyu', was made governor of Guang Province in 405 and was beaten in 411: Sun Chu held Panyu by the new year, Lu fled toward Jiao Province, was defeated by its governor Du Huidu and killed himself.
wars.note: Extent from the Sun En page (Kuaiji; Zhoushan) and the Emperor Wu of Liu Song page (Panyu 404-411). Lu Xun is Sun En's nephew on the Emperor Wu page and his brother-in-law on the Sun En page. Neither the rebel-held land nor Lu Xun's years as Guang Province's governor (405-409) is drawn: sun-en-rebellion has no dossier.

wars.outcome: Huan Xuan takes the throne in winter 403 and is overthrown by Liu Yu in 404.

notes:
CLIOPATRIA ROW. 'Western Jin' runs 265-425 in 19 shapes and covers both the Western Jin (266-316) and the Eastern Jin (317-420); the Wikipedia title is the whole Jin dynasty (266-420). This dossier treats them as one state: the Eastern Jin is a rename event at 317 with the same colour. Cliopatria's Liu Song row begins in 426, so 421-425 (the Western Jin shape of 417) are the liu-song-dynasty dossier's years. Wikidata Q7352 is not shared.
START AND END. 4 February 266 (the row starts 265) to 10 July 420 (Julian; the row runs to 425). The Wu conquest ends on 1 May 280 and Cliopatria draws the Wu land from 283; the shape of 283 holds from 280.
MAIN CORRECTIONS. (1) The Western Regions (2,266 Xinjiang and 125 Kyrgyz cells) are a vassal tint 266-328 with the Tarim city-states as counterpart (no dossier; the protectorate dossier of ea-02 draws nothing for 176-334, so it cannot be the counterpart), whose support is one sentence on a thin page (confidence 1; the 328 end is that sentence's 'around 328', tied to Li Bo of Former Liang). (2) Cliopatria's 313-336 shapes keep Gansu, Hebei, Shandong, Liaoning and the Huai country as Jin land after the fall of Chang'an in 316; the Jin infobox has the court 'south of the Huai River' from 317 (the sentence 'lost the north to the Sixteen Kingdoms' is on no page) and the Sixteen Kingdoms page a border 'along or above the Huai river', so the shape from 317 is the 337 shape (new keyframe western-jin_317; western-jin_324 is marked wrong), with Gansu and Liaoning as vassal tints. (3) 304-305: Cheng-Han and Han-Zhao left in 304, two years before Cliopatria. (4) New keyframes for Luoyang 356-364, Xiangyang lost 379-382, Guanzhong lost 418-420. (5) Sichuan and Chongqing are out of the shape 405-412 (Western Shu; western-jin_405 and _410) and back in 413 (western-jin_413). (6) Shandong stays Jin's to 393 (western-jin_387 and _390 adjusted): the Later Yan page has Later Yan capture it from the Eastern Jin after the 394 campaign, where Cliopatria hands it over in 387. (7) The Murong of the Liao are Jin vassals from 289 to 352 (Murong Hui and Sixteen Kingdoms pages).
GAPS (page silent). Unverified: the 276 Hebei and Henan cells of western-jin_390 and _394 (the Later Yan page puts the Zhai Wei there in 388-392, so they may not be Jin land) and the Southern Yan frontier of 402 (page budget). Sun En's rebels: Kuaiji (399-402) and Lu Xun's Panyu (captured 404, Lu governor of Guang Province from 405, beaten 411) are page-dated but not drawn, because the status of Lu Xun's Guang Province in 405-409 (a nominal Jin governor) is not settled and sun-en-rebellion has no dossier. The extent of Wang Dun's and Su Jun's rebellions (names only, no years on the page). The Qi Wannian revolt and the Tuyuhun (Cliopatria 287-323, a neighbour) are not on the pages opened; the Lâm Ấp page records Fan Wen's 347 attack on Jin Jiaozhou but no change of frontier, so champa's 347 gain of northern Rinan (Quảng Bình, confidence 1 there) has no mirror loss here. The Jin page's own areas (3.1 M km2 in 280, 2.8 M km2 in 347) are the only area check; Cliopatria's shape alive in 280 (western-jin_265, 2,972,633 km2) is 0.96 of the 3.1 M km2, this dossier's 280 shape (western-jin_283, 4,372,893 km2) is 1.41 of it (the infobox is 0.71 of the shape) and the 347 shape is 0.84 of 2.8 M km2: all within a factor of two.
DISAGREEMENTS. Min's reign: 313-316 (page table) against installed at Chang'an in 312 (Han-Zhao page). Sima Rui: 317 (infobox) against 318 (text). Sun Hao's surrender: 1 May 280 (Conquest page) against 31 May 280 (Eastern Wu infobox). Sun En's death: in battle in 401 (Emperor Wu page) against 'April or May 402' (Sun En page); Lu Xun is his nephew (Emperor Wu page) or brother-in-law (Sun En page). Emperor Huai's reign ends 311 (Jin page table) or 14 March 313 (his own page). The Western Shu rising: 'spring 405' (Emperor Wu page), 'Prince of Chengdu in 405' (Western Shu page). Cheng-Han: 304 (Li Xiong king of Chengdu) and 306 (emperor), Han-Zhao 304 (king) and 308 (emperor), both 'declared independence' in 304 on the Jin page. The 'Western Jin dynasty' URL returned the same article as the Jin dynasty page (a redirect), counted as a page opened but not as a second source.
BUDGET. Eleven content pages were opened against a budget of nine; the extra ones are the Chief Official and Protectorate pages (Western Regions), the Sixteen Kingdoms page (which stood in for four state pages) and the Lelang page (Korea), each shared with the cao-wei or counterpart work.
COUNTERPARTS WITHOUT A DOSSIER. Western Shu (western-shu, 405-413), the Tarim city-states (266-328), Yao Xiang's Luoyang (356), the Murong Xianbei before 337 (the former-yan dossier may start earlier; they are Jin vassals from 289), Sun En's rebels and Lu Xun's Guang Province (sun-en-rebellion, 399-411), Huan Xuan's Chu (403-404), the Jin loyalist governors of the north (Liu Kun, Wang Jun) named in no page opened.
REPAIR PASS (2026-10-19), after the adversarial review: Western Shu added (405 loss, 412-413 contest, new keyframes western-jin_405 and _413, _410 adjusted); the Murong vassal pair re-dated 289-352; the 317 loss re-sourced to the Jin infobox with former-zhao as counterpart; the Western Regions pair given the Tarim city-states as counterpart and ended about 328; eastern-wu added to the predecessors; Emperor Huai's reign extended to 313; Shandong's loss moved to 394 and the 387 and 390 shapes adjusted; Daifang re-sourced; Sun En's war extended to Lu Xun's Panyu (404-411); a war added for the Linyi attacks. Seven pages opened for the first time (Western Shu, Emperor Huai of Jin, Later Yan, Daifang Commandery, Murong Hui, Sun En, Lâm Ấp) and six re-read (Emperor Wu of Liu Song, Jin, Sixteen Kingdoms, Han-Zhao, Former Liang, Chief Official).
